comparisons.peer_summary: Multiple lawsuits alleging LIBOR manipulation by the Corporation, BANA, and other banks remain pending in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, with motions for summary judgment currently pending for remaining claims involving individual and class plaintiffs.
comparisons.comparison: While both Citigroup and Bank of America face antitrust litigation in the SDNY, the subject matter differs. Citigroup's litigation concerns interest rate swaps, whereas Bank of America's litigation concerns LIBOR manipulation. Both are industry-wide class actions consolidated in the SDNY, but Bank of America's claims remain pending with summary judgment motions, contrasting with Citigroup's class action which received preliminary settlement approval in 2024.

sentences.text: Beginning in 2015, Citigroup, Citibank, CGMI, CGML and numerous other parties were named as defendants in a number of industry-wide putative class actions related to interest rate swap (IRS) trading.
These actions have been consolidated in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York under the caption IN RE INTEREST RATE SWAPS ANTITRUST LITIGATION.
On July 11, 2024, the district court granted preliminary approval of the parties' settlement of the class action.
Beginning in 2011, several individual and putative class actions were filed against the Corporation, BANA, and certain Merrill Lynch entities, as well as other banks on the U.S. Dollar LIBOR panel.

These actions alleged that defendants manipulated LIBOR during the financial crisis and asserted a variety of claims, including federal and state antitrust, Commodity Exchange Act, Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, common law fraud, and breach of contract claims and sought compensatory, treble and punitive damages, and injunctive relief.

Defendants' motion for summary judgment is pending on all remaining claims, brought by individual plaintiffs and one class of plaintiffs who purchased over-the-counter instruments incorporating LIBOR.

sentences.text: Beginning in 2015, Citigroup, Citibank, CGMI, CGML and numerous other parties were named as defendants in a number of industry-wide putative class actions related to interest rate swap (IRS) trading.
On December 15, 2023, the court denied plaintiffs' motion for class certification.
On July 11, 2024, the district court granted preliminary approval of the parties' settlement of the class action.

Group Inc., GS&Co., GSI, GS Bank USA and Goldman Sachs Financial Markets, L.P. are among the defendants named in a putative antitrust class action relating to the trading of interest rate swaps, filed in November 2015 and consolidated in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

On December 15, 2023, the court denied the plaintiffs' motion for class certification, and on December 28, 2023, the plaintiffs filed a petition with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit seeking interlocutory review of the district court's denial of class certification.
On July 11, 2024, the court preliminarily approved a settlement among the plaintiffs and certain defendants, including the firm, to resolve the class action.

comparisons.peer_summary: The monetary relief class action settled for ~$6.2 billion with $700 million returned to defendants; a separate injunctive class action saw preliminary approval denied in June 2024, while individual actions by opting merchants have mostly settled representing over 70% of sales volume. Ongoing matters include a Swiss EURIBOR investigation and a U.S. Court of Appeals affirmation of a dismissal in an antitrust lawsuit; the Firm has resolved all non-U.S. dollar LIBOR actions and obtained dismissals or moved for summary judgment in remaining U.S. dollar LIBOR cases.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase face antitrust litigation in the SDNY, but the instruments and outcomes differ significantly. Citigroup's interest rate swap class action received preliminary settlement approval in July 2024, while JPMorgan's LIBOR-related antitrust claims saw the court grant class certification for certain bond and interest rate swap claims (referencing the BBA period). JPMorgan's disclosure focuses on settled interchange fee litigation and ongoing LIBOR/swap certification, whereas Citigroup's focuses on the settlement approval of the swap antitrust class action.
